quote: Weise vor Allem nach die Unendlichkeit solcher Prim-
english: Above all, prove the infinitude of such primes.
topic: Research plans: studying prime ideals following Kronecker via the field y^2+1=0, re-proving Gauss's representation of primes as sums of two squares via the function field x^2+y^2=p, proving Dirichlet's unit theorem without the existence theorem for roots, and counting primes for which 2 is a primitive root.

triage.modern_statement: Prove that infinitely many primes p have 2 as a primitive root mod p, i.e. that 2 generates the multiplicative group (Z/pZ)*. Put another way, the multiplicative order of 2 mod p is p−1 for infinitely many p. This is the case g = 2 of Artin's primitive root conjecture (Artin, 1927). The quantitative form of the conjecture also predicts the density of such primes (Artin's constant ≈ 0.3739).
triage.answered_by: Not answered unconditionally. C. Hooley (1967) proved it assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Gupta–Ram Murty (1984) and Heath-Brown (1986) proved unconditionally that at least one of 2, 3, 5 is a primitive root for infinitely many primes. That result does not settle the case g = 2. No specific integer g is known unconditionally to be a primitive root for infinitely many primes.

evidence.claim: Artin conjectured in 1927 that there are infinitely many primes for which g is a primitive root. Forty years later, Hooley showed that the conjecture follows from GRH.
No specific value of g is known to be a primitive root for infinitely many primes. Heath-Brown, refining Gupta and Murty, showed that at least one of 2, 3 and 5 has this property.
Artin's conjecture remains unsolved, and work in this direction continues, e.g. bounded gaps between primes with a given primitive root (conditional on GRH).
Moree's survey covers the extensive literature, including Hooley's method, Heath-Brown's 1986 result and many generalizations.

triage.why: The page topic says Hilbert planned to count primes for which 2 is a primitive root. The line 'prove the infinitude of such primes' is therefore the g = 2 case of what was later called Artin's primitive root conjecture. Artin stated it in 1927, which is after this diary entry. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The sources show it is still open without assumptions: it is proved only under GRH (Hooley 1967), and the unconditional result (Heath-Brown 1986) covers only 'at least one of 2, 3, 5'. Papers and surveys from 2014 onward show the area is still actively researched.
